y-m-13-01.title: I crossed out a digit and the answer was right
y-m-13-01.topic: Simplifying: whether the method of making the numerator and denominator simpler is valid
y-m-13-01.goal: Check with a counterexample that getting a right answer for one fraction is not a ground for the method being correct, and evaluate how reliable the method is by finding fractions that are right by chance.
y-m-13-01.material: To write the fraction 16/64 (16 over 64) in a simpler way, Harin crossed out the digit 6 that appears in both the numerator 16 and the denominator 64. With the remaining digits, the numerator is 1 and the denominator is 4, giving 1/4 (1 over 4), and 1/4 is equal in size to 16/64. Harin says, 'If you cross out the same digit, you can simplify a fraction.' Here, all fractions are fractions whose numerator and denominator are natural numbers.
y-m-13-01.thinking.0: Telling apart a result being right and a method being correct
y-m-13-01.thinking.1: Testing a generalization with a counterexample
y-m-13-01.thinking.2: Finding and verifying examples that fit the conditions yourself
y-m-13-01.prereq.0: Finding fractions equal in size (5th-grade level)
y-m-13-01.prereq.1: Multiplying a one-digit number and a two-digit number
y-m-13-01.s.s1.prompt: Read Harin's explanation line by line and choose one line where the thinking has a problem. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read by separating whether each line is a fact you can check by calculating or a statement judging that the method is correct.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find how far the lines that state only checkable facts go, and look at what the lines after that use as their ground.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.0: In 16/64, cross out the digit 6 that is in both the numerator and the denominator.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.1: The remaining digits are numerator 1 and denominator 4, so it becomes 1/4.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.2: 1/4 and 16/64 are equal in size. Because if you divide both 16 and 64 by 16, you get 1 and 4.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.3: The answer came out right, so the method of 'crossing out the same digit' is also a correct method.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore, for any fraction, if you cross out the digit that is in both the numerator and the denominator, you can simplify it.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.explain: The problems are on line 4 and line 5. Up to line 3, these are facts you can check by calculating directly (16/64=1/4). But getting the answer right for one fraction does not mean the method is always right. Line 5 widens the conclusion of line 4 to all fractions, so it is even more risky. In the next step, we check by using the same method on other fractions.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's use the same method on 12/21 (12 over 21). 12 and 21 both contain the digits 1 and 2. (12/21 is equal in size to 4/7.) Choose the suitable statement.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.0: For 12/21, write the result of crossing out the digit 1 and the result of crossing out the digit 2.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the results of crossing out are equal in size to 12/21, using the fact that 12/21 is equal to 4/7.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.a: Whether the digit crossed out is 1 or 2, the result is 2/2 or 1/1, which equals 1, so 12/21 must equal 1 too.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.a: You trusted the result of crossing out as it was. Compare the fact that 12/21 equals 4/7 with the results of crossing out.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.b: 12/21 is just an exception because it has a special shape where the digits of the numerator and denominator are swapped, and the method is always right for other fractions.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.b: You admit one exception but still think the method is always right. Did you check it on other fractions?
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.c: Depending on the digit crossed out, it becomes 2/2 or 1/1, and both differ in size from 12/21, so it is not a method that always works.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.c: You saw that changing the digit crossed out changes the result and that neither is equal to the original fraction. You know that one example can break 'always'.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.d: If we agree to cross out only the ones digit, the 1 is crossed out and it becomes 2/2, so this method becomes a correct method.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.d: You tried to protect the method by adding an agreement. Are 2/2 and 12/21 equal in size?
y-m-13-01.s.s2.explain: 12/21=4/7, but crossing out a digit makes 2/2 or 1/1, which differs in size from the original fraction. Harin's method happened to be right for 16/64 but is not right for 12/21. One counterexample breaks the claim that 'it is a method that is right for any fraction'.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.prompt: Let's find fractions for which Harin's method is right by chance. Think of fractions whose numerator is a two-digit number ab (tens digit a, ones digit b) and whose denominator is a two-digit number bc (tens digit b, ones digit c). If you cross out the same digit b in the middle, you get a/c. Enter 2 fractions, other than 16/64, for which the fraction a/c after crossing out is equal in size to the original fraction. a, b, c are digits from 1 to 9, and a and c are different.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write a/c yourself, and compare whether it is equal in size to the original fraction (10a+b)/(10b+c) by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.1: Set b to 9 and check by changing a and c one at a time.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.var.a: Tens digit a of the numerator
y-m-13-01.s.s3.var.b: Digit b to cross out (the ones digit of the numerator and also the tens digit of the denominator)
y-m-13-01.s.s3.var.c: Ones digit c of the denominator
y-m-13-01.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, c are digits from 1 to 9.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c1: a, b, c must all be digits from 1 to 9.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c2: If a and c are the same, it is a case like 11/11 where the size is 1 from the start, so it is excluded.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.ok.c3: It is a new example other than 16/64.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c3: 16/64 is an example you already saw. Find a different example.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.ok.c4: The fraction before crossing out and the fraction a/c after crossing out are equal in size.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c4: The fraction a/c after crossing out differs in size from the original fraction.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.explain: There are 19/95 (=1/5), 26/65 (=2/5), and 49/98 (=1/2). Including 16/64, there are only four such fractions. For most fractions, crossing out a digit changes the size. So crossing out digits is a method you can't trust, except for the cases that are right by chance.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.prompt: After searching, you found that there are very few such fractions. Write what you would like to tell Harin about the method of crossing out digits.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.hint.0: Think of one example like 12/21 where crossing out gave a wrong answer.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.hint.1: Thinking about how few fractions you found, examine whether the word 'always' is right.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Does the reason you gave include a concrete example, like 12/21 or a fraction you found?
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write telling apart 'the method is correct' and 'the answer was right this time'?
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.model.0: Harin's method is right by chance for some fractions like 16/64, but it is not always right. For 12/21, the value changes depending on which digit you cross out, and it also differs from 4/7. You should use the method of dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.model.1: The answer being right was by chance. There are only a few such fractions, like 19/95, 26/65, and 49/98. Most are wrong like 12/21, so you shouldn't trust crossing out digits.

y-m-13-02.title: Are there fractions between 1/3 and 1/2?
y-m-13-02.topic: Comparing fractions with different denominators and fractions between two fractions
y-m-13-02.goal: Check a claim made by looking only at the denominators, make several fractions that fit between two fractions yourself, and confirm them by comparing sizes.
y-m-13-02.material: Ara and her friend are talking about whether there is a fraction between 1/3 (1 over 3) and 1/2 (1 over 2). Ara: 'There is no natural number between the denominators 3 and 2. So there is no fraction at all between 1/3 and 1/2.' Here, fractions are fractions whose numerator and denominator are both natural numbers.
y-m-13-02.thinking.0: Checking a claim with no ground
y-m-13-02.thinking.1: Making several fractions that fit the conditions yourself
y-m-13-02.thinking.2: Confirming by comparison that the fractions you made meet the conditions
y-m-13-02.prereq.0: Finding fractions equal in size (5th-grade level)
y-m-13-02.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of fractions (5th-grade level)
y-m-13-02.s.s1.prompt: You want to find out whether Ara's words are right. What is worth doing first?
y-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.0: The fractions 1/3 and 2/3 have the same denominator. Are these two fractions equal in size?
y-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think of a way to change the two fractions into a form where you can compare their sizes at a glance.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.a: Check once more whether there really is no natural number between the denominators 3 and 2.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.a: You are only looking at the size of the denominators. The size of a fraction depends on both the denominator and the numerator. Even 1/3 and 2/3, which have the same denominator, differ in size.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.b: Change 1/3 and 1/2 into fractions with the same denominator and look for fractions that fit in between.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.b: You used the idea that if you make the denominators the same, you can compare the two fractions at a glance by the size of the numerators.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.c: Ara said it herself, so I trust it and don't examine separately whether there are fractions in between.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.c: You accepted it without checking the ground. The statement 'there is none at all' can be broken by one example.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.d: Estimate 1/3 and 1/2 as decimals and look for numbers that fit between the two.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.d: Changing to decimals to compare sizes is also a usable idea. But 1/3 is a non-terminating decimal, so an estimate is needed.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.explain: Even if the denominators 3 and 2 are neighbors, the size of a fraction is not decided by the denominator alone. You can check by changing the two fractions to the same denominator and seeing whether there is room for a numerator in between. Estimating with decimals can also be used.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.acc.0: If you estimate with decimals, you can see that there is a number like 0.4 between 0.333… and 0.5. But 1/3 is a non-terminating decimal so an estimate is needed, and you need to change it back to a fraction to check what fraction that number is (2/5).
y-m-13-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 fractions of different sizes that are greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2. Write a fraction with numerator a and denominator b, where the denominator b is a natural number that is 30 or less. Fractions of equal size (example: 2/5 and 4/10) count as one.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.0: First try, one at a time, whether any fraction with denominator 5 is greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing a denominator, change the numerator and check separately whether it is greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator and denominator are natural numbers and the denominator is 30 or less.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator and denominator must be natural numbers and the denominator must be 30 or less.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.explain: If you set the denominator to 30, 1/3 is 10/30 and 1/2 is 15/30. Between them are 11/30, 12/30 (=2/5), 13/30, and 14/30. Other fractions such as 3/7, 3/8, and 5/12 are also in between. Even when the denominators are neighbors, there are many fractions between the two fractions.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the fractions you just made, and write how you checked that it is greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2. Also add one sentence you would say to Ara.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write what 1/3 and 1/2 would look like if they were fractions with the same denominator.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.hint.1: Change the fraction you chose into a fraction with the same denominator too and write the three fractions side by side.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you change the fraction you chose, 1/3, and 1/2 into the same form (the same denominator or decimals) and put them side by side?
y-m-13-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the idea 'there is nothing between neighboring numbers' does not hold for fractions?
y-m-13-02.s.s3.model.0: I chose 2/5. If I make the denominator 30, 1/3 is 10/30, 1/2 is 15/30, and 2/5 is 12/30, so it is in between. Ara, even if the denominators are neighboring numbers, there are fractions in between.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.model.1: I chose 3/8. In decimals, 3/8 is 0.375, 1/3 is about 0.333, and 1/2 is 0.5, so it fits in between. Unlike what Ara said, there are fractions between 1/3 and 1/2.

y-m-13-03.title: If you put in parentheses, will the result definitely change?
y-m-13-03.topic: Mixed calculation with natural numbers: parentheses and the order of calculation
y-m-13-03.goal: Test the claim 'putting in parentheses always changes it', find a counterexample yourself, and explain the condition under which the result does not change.
y-m-13-03.material: Jiho said, 'If you put parentheses in an expression, the result always changes.' Sua answered, 'Is that really always so? I think there are cases where it doesn't change.' The two decided to compare two expressions using three numbers a, b, c. Expression ㉮ is a + b × c (a plus b times c), and expression ㉯ is (a + b) × c (first calculate a plus b, then multiply by c). All three numbers are natural numbers that are 1 or more, and they follow the agreement that multiplication is calculated before addition.
y-m-13-03.thinking.0: Understanding that one example cannot decide 'always'
y-m-13-03.thinking.2: Stating the condition for it to hold from what the examples have in common
y-m-13-03.prereq.0: The agreement to calculate multiplication first in an expression that mixes addition and multiplication
y-m-13-03.prereq.1: The agreement to calculate inside parentheses first when there are parentheses
y-m-13-03.s.s1.prompt: When a=2, b=3, c=4, ㉮ is 2 + 3 × 4 = 14 and ㉯ is (2 + 3) × 4 = 20. What can you say about the two people's words from this one example?
y-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether 14 and 20 show Jiho's words or Sua's words.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what kind of example you need to show that 'it is always so' is wrong.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.a: It changed once, so I can be sure Jiho's words are right for any three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.a: You widened one example to all cases. To check 'always', you need to look at all sets of three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.b: Parentheses do not affect the result, so Sua's words are right and Jiho's words are wrong.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.b: You have just seen the example that changed with 14 and 20. Look at whether this contradicts that example.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.c: If I change the three numbers a few more times and everything changes, Jiho's words are proven.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.c: Trying a few times is not the same as checking all cases. There are still sets of three numbers you haven't tried.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.d: Sua's words can be checked only by finding at least one set of three numbers for which the values are equal.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.d: You know that one opposite example is needed to break 'always'.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.explain: One example cannot check 'always'. Whether Sua's words are right is confirmed if you find even one set of three numbers for which the values of the two expressions are equal. Conversely, to prove Jiho's words, you would have to look at all sets of three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.prompt: Check Sua's words. Find and enter sets of three numbers (a, b, c) for which the values of a + b × c and (a + b) × c are equal. All three numbers are natural numbers from 1 to 20, and swapping only the places of a and b (example: (2, 5, 1) and (5, 2, 1)) counts as the same example. You need 3 different examples.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.0: First choose simple numbers for a and b, and write the values of the two expressions while changing c to 1, 2, 3.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.1: Collect the examples where the two expressions had equal values and look at which numbers are the same among them.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The three numbers are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c1: All three numbers must be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The value is equal even with parentheses.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The value changes when you put in parentheses.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.explain: In all three examples, c is 1. a + b × 1 = a + b and (a + b) × 1 = a + b, so the value is equal with or without parentheses. If c is not 1, in (a + b) × c, a also becomes c times as big, so the value changes.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.prompt: What do the three sets of numbers you found have in common? Using that, write how it would be good to fix Jiho's words.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the three examples you found side by side and find the letter that has the same value.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Also write one example of what happens when that letter has a different value.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check where the same part is in all three sets of numbers you found?
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is Jiho's corrected statement accurate even without the word 'always'?
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.model.0: In all three sets of numbers I found, c was 1. Multiplying by 1 leaves it as it is, so it is the same with or without parentheses. So Jiho's words should be fixed to 'when c is not 1', not 'always'.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.model.1: When the multiplier (c) is 1, the two expressions were equal. They were different for other numbers, so Jiho's words are right only when the multiplier is not 1.

y-m-13-04.title: They said about 800 people, but how many were there really?
y-m-13-04.topic: Estimating numbers: guessing the range of the real number from a rounded value
y-m-13-04.goal: Reason out the range the real number could be in when you know only the rounded value, and revise the range and how sure you are each time information is added.
y-m-13-04.material: You are finding out the number of users of a library last month. The number of users is a natural number. The values written in several places might have been estimated by different methods. Rounding is a method where, if the digit just below the place you want is 5 or more you round up, and if it is 4 or less you round down.
y-m-13-04.thinking.0: Reasoning out the range of the real number from an estimated value
y-m-13-04.thinking.1: Narrowing the range with new information
y-m-13-04.thinking.2: Deciding how to judge when you meet pieces of information that don't match
y-m-13-04.prereq.1: Expressing ranges of numbers, like 'or more' and 'less than'
y-m-13-04.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think about the real number of users.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, first write the smallest and the largest number that the number before rounding could be.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put the two ranges side by side on a number line or as a list of numbers and find the overlapping part.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The sign at the library entrance says 'Users last month: about 800 (rounded to the hundreds place).'
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most suitable thing to say about the real number of users?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.after: The natural numbers that become 800 when rounded to the hundreds place are 750 to 849. 750 becomes 800 by rounding up, and 849 becomes 800 by rounding down.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is 800 people or more and less than 900 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought of it like the range for rounding down. If you round, 790 people also becomes 800 people. Is 790 people in this range?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It is an estimated value, so you can't say it equals the real number.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is more than 700 people and 800 people or less.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought of it like the range for rounding up. Rounding sometimes rounds up and sometimes rounds down.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is 750 people or more and less than 850 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You turned the rule 'round up if the lower digit is 5 or more, round down if it is 4 or less' into a range.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.info: The library website says 'Users last month: about 840 (rounded to the tens place).'
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: If you consider both pieces of information to be right, what can you say about the real number of users?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The natural numbers that become 840 when rounded to the tens place are 835 to 844. These numbers are all inside the earlier 750~849, so looking at the two pieces of information together, the real number narrows to 835~844 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is 750 people or more and less than 850 people. The new information does not change the range.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You did not use the new information. Think about the range of numbers near 840 that become 840 when rounded.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is 835 people or more and less than 845 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You kept only the part where the ranges given by the two pieces of information overlap. You narrowed the range with the new information.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You treated the estimated value as the real number.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is 840 people or more and less than 850 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You thought of rounding to the tens place like rounding up or rounding down. What does 836 people become when rounded?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.info: The library's guide booklet gives an exact number, 'Users: 846'. It is not certain whether this booklet counted last month's users.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How is it good to take in this new information?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If you don't know whether the booklet counted users of the same month, you can't overturn the earlier conclusion based on 846. If it is the same month, 846 and 'about 840 by rounding' can't both be right, so you need to check the estimating method or the counting period. Keeping the range as it is and waiting for confirmation, or deciding what to check and revising your thinking, are both suitable.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: I don't know whether it is a figure for the same month, so I keep the range 835~844 and think again once it is confirmed.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You first examined whether the new information counted the same thing. You kept your judgment while leaving a condition for revising it.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 846 is an exactly counted number, so I consider both earlier pieces of information wrong and throw them out.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You threw out all the earlier information without even checking whether it was the same month.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If it is the same month, one of the two is off, so I check the website's estimating method or counting period first.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You noticed that the new information and the earlier information can't both be right, and decided what to check.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 846 rounded to the tens place is 850, so I conclude that the website's 840 is wrong.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You concluded that one side was wrong without checking whether the website used rounding or whether it was the same month.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.reflect: As information was added one piece at a time, how did the possible range change? When you met the last piece of information, what did you use to decide whether to change the earlier conclusion?
y-m-13-04.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different numbers of users (natural numbers) that fit both pieces of information (840 when rounded to the tens place, and 800 when rounded to the hundreds place).
y-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.0: Move up and down one step at a time from 840 and check whether the rounded result is 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.1: At the bottom and top of the range, check separately whether the boundary numbers are included.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Rounded to the tens place, it is 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Rounded to the tens place, it does not become 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Rounded to the hundreds place, it is 800.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Rounded to the hundreds place, it does not become 800.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.explain: All of 835 to 844 are right. For 835~839 the ones digit is 5 or more, so they round up to 840, and for 840~844 the ones digit is 4 or less, so they round down to 840. These numbers are also 800 when rounded to the hundreds place.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Write the smallest and the largest number of users you can make, and explain why they are so.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Round 834 and 845 each to the tens place.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write in one sentence why the two numbers at the ends of the range are distinguished from the numbers outside.

y-m-13-05.title: 5/6 + 3/8: comparing four methods
y-m-13-05.topic: Adding fractions: comparing several ways to add two fractions with different denominators
y-m-13-05.goal: Among several methods for finding the sum of two fractions with different denominators, pick out the ones that can be used, and make examples to explain when two correct methods are the same and when they differ.
y-m-13-05.material: You want to add 5/6 (5 over 6) and 3/8 (3 over 8). Four friends each said a different method. One friend said to add the numerators 5+3=8 and the denominators 6+8=14 to get 8/14. Another friend said to make the denominator 6×8=48 and calculate 40/48 + 18/48. Another friend said to make the denominator 24, a common multiple of 6 and 8, and calculate 20/24 + 9/24. The last friend thought of 5/6 as about 0.83 and 3/8 as about 0.38 and said the sum is about 1.2.
y-m-13-05.thinking.0: Comparing the validity of several solution methods
y-m-13-05.thinking.1: Making cases yourself where two methods differ
y-m-13-05.thinking.2: Explaining the strengths and weaknesses of methods in words
y-m-13-05.prereq.1: Adding fractions with the same denominator
y-m-13-05.prereq.2: Finding common multiples of two numbers (5th-grade level)
y-m-13-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the methods that can be used to find the value of 5/6 + 3/8 as an exact fraction.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write what form each method changes the two fractions into, and check whether the denominators became the same.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the result from each method is bigger or smaller than 5/6 alone.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.a: Add the numerators and add the denominators to get 8/14.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.a: If you add the denominators, the size of one piece changes, so you are no longer counting pieces of the same size. Compare whether 8/14 is bigger or smaller than 5/6.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.b: You used the idea of changing the two fractions into the same size of pieces and adding.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.c: Estimate 5/6 and 3/8 as decimals and say it is about 1.2.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.c: An estimate tells you roughly what the value is, but it does not give an exact fraction. It is useful for checking.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.d: Make the denominator 24, a common multiple of 6 and 8, and add.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.d: You used the idea of choosing the smaller common multiple to keep the numbers small.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.explain: Whether you make the denominator 48 or 24, you change them into pieces of the same size and add, so the sum is the same (58/48 = 29/24). 8/14, from adding numerators and denominators separately, is even smaller than 5/6, so it can't be the sum. An estimate is not an exact value, but it can be used to check whether a calculation is right.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.acc.0: The method of estimating with decimals does not give an exact fraction value, but it is valid as a way to find out roughly what the sum is. If you need an exact value, you should use b or d.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 pairs of denominators (p, q) for which the method of making the denominator by multiplying and the method of using the smallest common multiple give different denominators. Like 6 and 8, p and q are natural numbers from 2 to 12, and p is less than q.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find the product and the smallest common multiple of the two denominators and write them side by side.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write separately the pairs of denominators for which the product and the common multiple were the same and the pairs for which they differed, and find the difference.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c2: p must be less than q.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The product and the smallest common multiple are different.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The product and the smallest common multiple are the same, so the two methods give the same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.explain: For 6 and 8, the product is 48 but the smallest common multiple is 24, so they are different. The same is true for 4 and 6 (product 24, common multiple 12) and 4 and 12 (product 48, common multiple 12). For two numbers that have no number besides 1 that divides both evenly, like 3 and 5, or 5 and 7, the product is itself the smallest common multiple, so the two methods give the same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.prompt: You can get the right answer by making the denominator by multiplying, but write what is convenient about using the smallest common multiple. Also give one example of two denominators for which the two methods give the same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.0: For 6 and 8, write the denominators you get from each of the two methods.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.1: Pick from the results of s2 the pairs of denominators where the two methods' denominators were the same.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For the two denominators you gave as an example, did you find the product and the smallest common multiple yourself and check whether they are the same?
y-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason 'convenient' concretely, such as less calculation?
y-m-13-05.s.s3.model.0: If you use the smaller common multiple, the numerators and denominators are small, so the calculation is easy, and at the end you don't have to simplify as much. Two denominators like 3 and 5, which have only 1 as a number that divides both evenly, have a product equal to the smallest common multiple.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.model.1: If you use the product of the denominators, the numbers get bigger, so the calculation is long and you may need more simplifying at the end. When the product is itself the smallest common multiple, like 5 and 7, the two methods give the same denominator.

y-m-13-06.title: The height of a bean sprout: what about ten days later?
y-m-13-06.topic: Finding a rule in change shown in a table and how much to trust the rule
y-m-13-06.goal: Guess what will happen using a rule found in the table, but revise your guess and how much you trust it when data increases, and say that the rule may be right only in the range that has been checked.
y-m-13-06.material: A kidney bean sprout is growing in a pot by the classroom window. Seojin measures the sprout's height (cm) every morning at the same time and writes it in a table. She writes the height rounded to a whole number. I will tell you at each step how many days have been measured so far.
y-m-13-06.thinking.0: Finding the rule of change in a table
y-m-13-06.thinking.1: Revising how sure you are when data increases
y-m-13-06.thinking.2: Considering the range where a rule applies
y-m-13-06.prereq.0: Reading a table and explaining how two quantities change together
y-m-13-06.prereq.1: Addition and multiplication of natural numbers
y-m-13-06.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think about the sprout's height.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write next to the table how much the height changed between each pair of days.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the number of days you have measured so far with the distance to the day you want to guess.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Day 1 is 4cm, day 2 is 6cm, day 3 is 8cm.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: If the same pattern continues, what is the most suitable thing to say about the height on day 7?
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.after: Day 1 4cm, day 2 6cm, day 3 8cm, so it grew 2cm per day. If this continues, day 7 is 4+2×6=16cm. But it is too early to fix the rule from just 3 days, so guess 'about 16cm'.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: About 28cm. Because you find it by multiplying the first height 4cm by the number of days.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: On day 2 it should be 4×2=8cm, but the table says 6cm. A multiplying rule does not match the table.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There are only 3 days, so you can't guess the height on day 7 at all.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Even if it isn't certain, the data gives a clue. You can look at how many cm it changed per day.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: About 16cm. It seems to grow 2cm per day, but we should watch longer.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You used the clue that the amount of change is constant, but you were not yet sure.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 16cm. Because the rule of growing 2cm per day is certain.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The value you guessed is the same, but you fixed the rule from 3 days. Think about whether there is a reason to keep watching.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.info: Day 4 is 10cm, day 5 is 12cm, day 6 is 14cm.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what has become of your thinking about the height on day 7?
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.after: The same rule continued for 6 days, so the guess of 16cm on day 7 became more trustworthy than at first. The guess stayed the same, and only how much you trust it grew. Still, you can't fix a day that has not been measured yet.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I see it as about 16cm, and since the rule was right for 6 days, I trust it more.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You read the new data as supporting the first rule. You kept your guess and raised how much you trust it.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I fixed it as 16cm, so I don't need to measure directly on day 7.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even if it was right for 6 days, there is no guarantee the same thing happens on day 7.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The data increased, so I throw away the first guess and change it to 12cm.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The new data matches the first rule. Look at whether there is a reason to change your guess.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is certain that on day 20 it will also grow 2cm a day and be 42cm.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: It is too early to be sure about day 20 from 6 days of data. Compare the number of days you checked with the number of days you want to guess.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Day 7 is 15cm, day 8 is 15cm, day 9 is 15cm. You can't tell whether the sprout stopped growing or the tip of the stem broke.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What do you think about the height on day 10 and the rule you found earlier?
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.after: Up to day 6 it was 2cm a day, but from day 7 the rule did not continue. It is suitable to revise your thinking so that the earlier rule was right only 'up to the days checked', guess day 10 to be near 15cm, and keep measuring.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The data for days 7~9 must have been measured wrongly, so I ignore it and guess 22cm for day 10.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You threw away the new data because it did not match the rule. New data can also be true.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: I think it is certain that now the height will stay 15cm forever.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even if it stopped for 3 days, you don't know why, so you can't be sure it will keep being so.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Nothing can be known, so guessing the height on day 10 is meaningless.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: That the rule changed is also important information. You can guess with that information.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I see the rule as right only up to day 6, guess near 15cm, and keep watching.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You revised your thinking so that the rule was right only up to the days checked, and decided to keep watching the parts you don't know.
y-m-13-06.s.s1.reflect: At each step, how did your guess for day 7 or day 10 and how much you trusted it change? Why shouldn't you promise it will be right in the future just because the same rule was right many times?
y-m-13-06.s.s2.prompt: Looking only at the table, a friend said, 'If it follows the rule, it will be 62cm on day 30!' Write what you would like to tell this friend.
y-m-13-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write the last day in the table when the rule was right and what happened after that.
y-m-13-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether the statement 62cm should be called a 'certain fact' or a 'guess'.
y-m-13-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your statement include the concrete fact that the rule was right up to day 6?
y-m-13-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say the height on day 30 is 'just a guess' rather than 'unknown'?
y-m-13-06.s.s2.model.0: Up to day 6 it was right at 2cm a day, but from day 7 it stopped at 15cm. You can't claim the rule continues, so 62cm on day 30 is not certain.
y-m-13-06.s.s2.model.1: The 2cm-a-day rule was right only up to the days checked in the table. Plants may not keep growing at the same speed, so 62cm is only a guess.

y-m-13-07.title: 5 copies for 400원: how much is one copy?
y-m-13-07.topic: Correspondence between two quantities: a price that may have a base fee
y-m-13-07.goal: Understand that the price rule cannot be fixed as just one from a single piece of data, make several possible price tables, and say what more information is needed.
y-m-13-07.material: Jimin made 5 copies at the copy shop in front of school and paid 400원. This shop charges the same extra price per copy as the number of copies increases. There may or may not be a base fee that is paid just once regardless of the number of copies. All values are in units of 10원. Jimin said, 'If you divide 400원 equally among 5 copies, it's 80원 per copy.'
y-m-13-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the data is enough
y-m-13-07.thinking.1: Making several rules that fit the conditions yourself
y-m-13-07.thinking.2: Saying what additional information settles the judgment
y-m-13-07.prereq.0: Showing a relationship in which two quantities change together as a table
y-m-13-07.prereq.1: Multiplication and division of natural numbers
y-m-13-07.s.s1.prompt: Is it okay to fix the price per copy at 80원 as Jimin said?
y-m-13-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think about the case where the base fee is 0원 and the case where it is 100원, and compare how much one copy must cost for 5 copies to be 400원.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the price per copy is the same or different in the two cases.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.o.a: It is 80원 only when there is no base fee, and if you don't know whether there is one, you can't decide.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.r.a: You know that the answer can differ depending on whether there is a base fee or not.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.o.b: 400원 is divided equally among 5 copies, so 80원 per copy is right.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.r.b: If there is a base fee, not all 400원 is the price by number of copies.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.o.c: There may be a base fee, so we can decide that the price per copy is less than 80원.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.r.c: 'There may be' and 'there is' are different. If there is no base fee, how many 원 is one copy?
y-m-13-07.s.s1.o.d: From the price of 5 copies made once alone, you can't even know whether the price goes up when the number of copies increases.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.r.d: The problem says that as the number of copies increases, the same extra price is charged per copy.
y-m-13-07.s.s1.explain: If there is no base fee, one copy is 80원 from 5 copies for 400원. But if there is a base fee, part of the 400원 is the base fee, so one copy is less than 80원. If you don't know whether there is a base fee, you can't fix the price per copy as one value.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different price tables in which 5 copies cost 400원. Decide and enter the price per copy p원 and the base fee b원. p is 40원 or more, b is 0원 or more and 200원 or less, and both are in units of 10원.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.hint.0: Set the base fee to 0원, 50원, 100원, and find how many 원 the price of 5 copies must be.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.hint.1: Look at how the base fee must change when you change the price per copy so that 400원 is kept.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.ok.c1: p and b are numbers in units of 10원 within the condition range.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.fail.c1: p must be 40 or more, b must be 0 or more and 200 or less, and both must be in units of 10원.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The price of 5 copies is not 400원. Check whether the base fee plus the price of 5 copies is 400원.
y-m-13-07.s.s2.explain: (80원, 0원), (70원, 50원), (60원, 100원), (50원, 150원), (40원, 200원) all give 400원 for 5 copies. Each time the price per copy goes down by 10원, the base fee goes up by 50원. From the price of 5 copies alone, you can't decide which of these price tables it is.
y-m-13-07.s.s3.prompt: To fix the price per copy as one value, what one more piece of information would Jimin need to have? Also write how you can decide with that information.
y-m-13-07.s.s3.hint.0: Find how many 원 it would be to make 1 copy in each of two possible price tables.
y-m-13-07.s.s3.hint.1: If the price for 1 copy comes out different, think about whether you can tell the price tables apart by that.
y-m-13-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the one piece of information you gave settles both p and b?
y-m-13-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If you use the price for a different number of copies, did you write concretely how to compare it with the price of 5 copies?
y-m-13-07.s.s3.model.0: It is enough to know the money paid for a different number of copies. For example, if you know the money paid for 1 copy, you can compare with 400원 for 5 copies to find the price of 4 copies, and from that you can fix the price per copy.
y-m-13-07.s.s3.model.1: It is enough to know whether there is a base fee, and if so, how much. Subtract the base fee from 400원 and divide the rest by 5 copies, and you get the price per copy.

y-m-13-08.title: Ways to use the pool: which is cheaper?
y-m-13-08.topic: Comparing how the total amount changes in two pricing methods (correspondence by number of visits)
y-m-13-08.goal: Compare in a table how the total amount of two pricing methods changes with the number of visits, explain that which one is better depends on the conditions, and find the number of visits that is the boundary.
y-m-13-08.material: You want to use the neighborhood swimming pool for one month. There are two ways to use it. Method 가: you pay 1500원 each time you go. Method 나: you pay the 5000원 membership for the month once, and pay 1000원 more each time you go. The fee for one visit is the same regardless of how many times you go. The number of visits in a month is a natural number from 1 to 30. In the table, for 1 visit Method 가 is 1500원 and Method 나 is 6000원, and for 2 visits Method 가 is 3000원 and Method 나 is 7000원.
y-m-13-08.thinking.0: Comparing two changes with a table
y-m-13-08.thinking.1: Stating a conclusion that changes depending on conditions
y-m-13-08.thinking.2: Finding the value that is the boundary
y-m-13-08.prereq.0: Showing the correspondence of two quantities in a table
y-m-13-08.prereq.1: Multiplication and addition of natural numbers, comparing the size of two numbers
y-m-13-08.s.s1.prompt: Which method has the smaller total cost over a month?
y-m-13-08.s.s1.hint.0: Continue the table to 3 visits, 4 visits, 5 visits… and look at how the difference between the totals of 가 and 나 changes.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find in the table whether there is a number of visits at which Method 나 becomes cheaper than Method 가.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.o.a: Method 나 is always cheaper. Because the money paid for one visit is less.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.r.a: There is a 5000원 paid at the start. Compare the totals of the two methods when you go only 1 time.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.o.b: Method 가 is always cheaper. Because you don't pay the 5000원 membership separately.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.r.b: With each visit, Method 가 pays more. Think about the case of going a very large number of times.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.o.c: It depends on the number of visits. We need to find out from the table from which number it changes.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.r.c: You saw that the money paid at the start and the money paid each time work in opposite ways.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.o.d: The totals of the two methods are always the same regardless of the number of visits.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.r.d: At 1 visit and 2 visits in the table, the two totals are already different.
y-m-13-08.s.s1.explain: Method 나 pays 5000원 first, but pays 500원 less than Method 가 for each visit. So if you go few times, Method 가 can be better, and if you go many times, Method 나 can be better. We check in the table at how many visits it changes.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.prompt: Say you go n times in a month (n is a natural number from 1 to 30). Find 3 different values of n for which the total amount of Method 나 is less than the total amount of Method 가.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.hint.0: Find in the table where the difference between the two totals shrinks, and find the number of visits at which the difference becomes 0.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check which side is cheaper when it is one visit fewer than that number and one visit more.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 30.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 1 to 30.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The total amount of Method 나 is less.
y-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The total amount of Method 나 is not less (it is equal or more).
y-m-13-08.s.s2.explain: From 11 visits to 30 visits, Method 나 is cheaper in every case. At 10 visits, Method 가 is 15000원 and Method 나 is 5000+10000=15000원, so they are equal and not included. At 9 visits or fewer, Method 가 is cheaper.
y-m-13-08.s.s3.prompt: Write what the amounts of the two methods are when you go exactly 10 times in a month, and write by what standard you would tell a friend to choose a method.
y-m-13-08.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate 10 visits for 가 and 나 each, and write them side by side.
y-m-13-08.s.s3.hint.1: Separate fewer than 10 visits and more than 10 visits and write one sentence each on which method is cheaper.
y-m-13-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show the equations or numbers for calculating the 10-visit value for 가 and 나 each?
y-m-13-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write it as a standard a friend can use right away, like 'if it's this many times, this side'?
y-m-13-08.s.s3.model.0: If you go 10 times, 가 is 15000원 and 나 is 5000+10000=15000원, exactly the same. If you will go more than 10 times, Method 나 is cheaper, and if fewer, Method 가 is cheaper.
y-m-13-08.s.s3.model.1: At 10 visits, the two methods are the same, 15,000원. So I'd tell them to first decide how many times they will go in a month, and choose 나 if it's 11 or more, and 가 if it's 9 or fewer.

y-m-13-09.title: The taste of 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water: will it be the same if we make more?
y-m-13-09.topic: The relationship of two quantities that increase together: making the same taste by increasing by the same multiple
y-m-13-09.goal: Tell apart adding the same number to two quantities and increasing two quantities by the same multiple, and make several combinations with the same taste by setting up a rule.
y-m-13-09.material: You like the taste of juice made by mixing 2 cups of juice concentrate with 3 cups of water, and you want to make more. All the cups are the same size. The taste of the mixed juice is decided only by the relationship between the number of cups of concentrate and water. Hajun said, 'I added 2 cups each to both the concentrate and the water, so if I mix 4 cups of concentrate and 5 cups of water, the taste will be the same!'
y-m-13-09.thinking.0: Finding the error in a plausible explanation
y-m-13-09.thinking.1: Telling apart adding and increasing by a multiple
y-m-13-09.thinking.2: Making several combinations that fit the rule
y-m-13-09.prereq.0: Reading a table and explaining the change of two quantities
y-m-13-09.s.s1.prompt: Read Hajun's explanation line by line and choose the line where the thinking has a problem. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-13-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write how many times the first amount the concentrate became and how many times the first amount the water became.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the two multiples are the same or different.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.line.0: At first it is 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.line.1: If you put in 2 more cups of concentrate, it becomes 4 cups.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.line.2: If you put in 2 more cups of water, it becomes 5 cups.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.line.3: I added the same 2 cups to the concentrate and the water, so the taste is the same as at first.
y-m-13-09.s.s1.explain: Line 4 has the problem. The concentrate doubled from 2 cups to 4 cups, but the water went from 3 cups to 5 cups and did not double (6 cups). Even if you add the same amount to two quantities, their relationship does not stay the same. To get the same taste, you must increase the concentrate and water by the same multiple.

y-m-13-09.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how many times each combination is a bundle of 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water.
y-m-13-09.s.s2.hint.1: Set a standard for how many cups of water are needed for every 2 cups of concentrate and compare each combination.
y-m-13-09.s.s2.o.a: 3 cups of concentrate, 4 cups of water

y-m-13-09.s.s2.o.b: 4 cups of concentrate, 6 cups of water

y-m-13-09.s.s2.o.c: 5 cups of concentrate, 6 cups of water

y-m-13-10.title: What day of the week is the 100th day from today?
y-m-13-10.topic: A repeating rule: the relationship in which the days of the week repeat every 7 days
y-m-13-10.goal: Do date calculations using the repeating rule of the days of the week, but understand that the answer differs depending on how you count the days and answer by stating the conditions.
y-m-13-10.material: Today is Thursday. The days of the week repeat every 7 days in the order Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed. Seoyeon and Jimin each calculated 'What day of the week is the 100th day from today?' without flipping through a calendar, and one said Friday and one said Saturday, so they were surprised at each other.
y-m-13-10.thinking.0: Finding the condition that causes the answers to differ
y-m-13-10.thinking.1: Making days with the same day of the week using the repeating rule
y-m-13-10.thinking.2: Explaining both answers by stating the conditions
y-m-13-10.prereq.0: A week is 7 days and the days of the week repeat in order
y-m-13-10.prereq.1: Division of natural numbers and remainders
y-m-13-10.s.s1.prompt: The two people's answers were different. To fix the day of the week of the 100th day as one, what is the first thing you need to know more?
y-m-13-10.s.s1.hint.0: When today is Thursday, write what day of the week 'day 1' and '1 day later' each are.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare where the two people start counting 100, to see if they counted different days.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.o.a: What month and date today is, and what year this year is
y-m-13-10.s.s1.r.a: The days of the week repeat every 7 days, so knowing that today is Thursday is enough. The date is not needed.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.o.b: Whether the '100th day' is counted with today as day 1 or with today as day 0
y-m-13-10.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that if the way of counting is different, there can be a one-day difference.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.o.c: Whether this year is a leap year so February has 29 days or not
y-m-13-10.s.s1.r.c: A leap year changes the number of days in February, but what day of the week it is some days later is decided by the rule that repeats every 7 days.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.o.d: How many holidays, which are days off, fall within the 100 days
y-m-13-10.s.s1.r.d: Even with holidays, the days of the week continue in order.
y-m-13-10.s.s1.explain: If you count the '100th day' with today as day 1, it is 99 days from today, and if you count with today as day 0, the 100th day is 100 days later. Depending on the way of counting there is a one-day difference, so the day of the week differs.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.prompt: Like Jimin, count with today as day 0 and say 'n days from today'. Find 3 different values of n that give the same day of the week as 100 days later. (n is a natural number from 1 to 60)
y-m-13-10.s.s2.hint.0: If you group 100 days into 7-day bundles, write how many bundles there are and how many days are left over.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find the days with the same number of leftover days and check by adding 7 at a time.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 60.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 1 to 60.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.ok.c2: It is the same day of the week as 100 days later.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.fail.c2: It is a different day of the week from 100 days later.
y-m-13-10.s.s2.explain: 100 days later is the day after 7 days pass 14 times and 2 more days pass, so it is Saturday, 2 days after Thursday. So the days made by adding 7 days at a time, like 2 days later, 9 days later, 16 days later, are all the same day of the week (Saturday).
y-m-13-10.s.s3.prompt: To say that both Seoyeon's and Jimin's answers can be right, write how each of them counted the '100th day' and what day of the week each person's answer is.
y-m-13-10.s.s3.hint.0: If today is day 1, write how many days from today the 100th day is.
y-m-13-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how many days beyond Thursday 99 days later and 100 days later each are.
y-m-13-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect each day of the week to the number of days later it counted (99 days later, 100 days later) with numbers?
y-m-13-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain it as 'the way of counting was different' rather than 'one person was wrong'?
y-m-13-10.s.s3.model.0: The person who set today as day 0 and counted 100 days later gets Saturday. The person who counted today as day 1 and looked at 99 days later gets Friday. The answer differs depending on how you count.
y-m-13-10.s.s3.model.1: If you think of it as '100 days later', it's Saturday, and if you think of it as the '100th day' counting today as day 1, it's Friday. The way of counting is different, so both can be right.

y-m-13-11.title: If we enlarge a square, what happens to the perimeter and area?
y-m-13-11.topic: The relationship of how a square's side and its perimeter and area change
y-m-13-11.goal: Investigate with several examples how many times the perimeter and the area become when a side becomes some number of times, find the rule between the multiple of a side and the multiple of the area, and explain why.
y-m-13-11.material: Doyun said, 'If you double one side of a square, the perimeter doubles and the area doubles too.' Here, the square has a side length that is a natural number of cm, and the unit of area is square centimeters (cm²).
y-m-13-11.thinking.1: Finding a rule from several examples
y-m-13-11.thinking.2: Explaining the reason using length and width
y-m-13-11.prereq.0: Finding the perimeter of a square (4th-grade level)
y-m-13-11.prereq.1: Finding the area of rectangles and squares (5th-grade level)
y-m-13-11.s.s1.prompt: A square with a side of 3cm was enlarged so that the side is 6cm. How many times the original will the perimeter and the area each be?
y-m-13-11.s.s1.hint.0: Find the perimeter and area for a side of 3cm and for a side of 6cm and write them in a table.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.hint.1: Put the original values and the values after enlarging side by side and find how many times they became.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.o.a: The perimeter is 2 times, the area is 4 times
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.a: You confirmed by calculating that when a side doubles, the perimeter and the area change by different multiples.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.o.b: The perimeter is 2 times, the area is 2 times too
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.b: This is the same as Doyun's words. Find the original area 3×3 and the area after enlarging 6×6 yourself and compare them.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.o.c: The perimeter is 4 times, the area is 4 times
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.c: The perimeter is the sum of the lengths of the four sides. Find how many cm the original perimeter of 12cm becomes after enlarging.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.o.d: The perimeter is 2 times, the area is 3 times
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.d: The area is found by multiplying the length and the width. Look at what happens to the length and the width when a side doubles.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.explain: When a side is 3cm, the perimeter is 12cm and the area is 9cm², and when a side is 6cm, the perimeter is 24cm and the area is 36cm². The perimeter is 2 times, but the area is 4 times. Doyun's 'the area doubles too' is not right in this example.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.prompt: The area of a square whose side is enlarged to k times the original becomes m times the original area. (k is a natural number from 2 to 10.) Enter 3 different correct pairs (k, m). You may also check by finding the area of the square yourself.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write in order the areas of squares with sides of 1cm, 2cm, 3cm, 4cm and find how many times each became.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.hint.1: Write in a table the multiples of the area when a side is 2 times and 3 times, and find the relationship between the two multiples.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.var.k: How many times the original is the side
y-m-13-11.s.s2.var.m: How many times the original is the area
y-m-13-11.s.s2.ok.c1: k is a natural number from 2 to 10.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.fail.c1: k must be a natural number from 2 to 10.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.ok.c2: When a side is k times, the area being m times is right.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.fail.c2: When a side is k times, the area is not m times. Check by calculating yourself.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.explain: If a side is 2 times, the area is 4 times; if 3 times, 9 times; if 4 times, 16 times; if 5 times, 25 times. When a side becomes k times, both the length and the width become k times, so the area becomes k×k times. The perimeter becomes only k times.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.prompt: Write the rule in words for how many times the area becomes when a side becomes k times, and explain why using the length and the width.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.hint.0: First write how many times the length and how many times the width become when a side is 2 times.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.hint.1: Use the fact that multiplying the multiple of the length by the multiple of the width gives the multiple of the area.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that your rule fits the area multiples for both 2 times and 3 times?
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is the reason that both the length and the width grow connected to the rule?
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.model.0: When a side becomes k times, the area becomes k×k times. The length becomes k times and the width becomes k times too, so you multiply the same number twice.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.model.1: When a side becomes 3 times, the area becomes 3×3=9 times. The length becomes 3 times and the width becomes 3 times too, so you multiply 3 twice.

y-m-13-12.title: If the pages read double, will the pages left be halved?
y-m-13-12.topic: A relationship where the sum is constant in two quantities that change together, and checking a generalization
y-m-13-12.goal: Using a table and counterexamples, find the error of widening a statement that was right in one case to all cases, and correctly rewrite the relationship that always holds between pages read and pages left.
y-m-13-12.material: A storybook has 120 pages in all. As the pages read increase, the pages left decrease. Below is a table of pages read and pages left. When pages read are 20, pages left are 100; when pages read are 40, pages left are 80; when pages read are 60, pages left are 60; when pages read are 80, pages left are 40; when pages read are 100, pages left are 20; when pages read are 120, pages left are 0. Chaea looked at the table and said, 'When the pages read double, the pages left are halved.'
y-m-13-12.thinking.0: Finding the error of generalizing something that was right in one case
y-m-13-12.thinking.2: Rewriting it as a relationship that always holds
y-m-13-12.prereq.0: Reading a table and explaining how two quantities change together
y-m-13-12.prereq.1: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication of natural numbers
y-m-13-12.s.s1.prompt: This is what Chaea said to explain her statement. Read it line by line and choose one line that has a problem. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-13-12.s.s1.hint.0: Find how the pages left change when the pages read double from 20 pages to 40 pages in the table.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.hint.1: Check in the same way from other starting page numbers in the table.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.0: When the pages read are 40, the pages left are 80.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.1: When the pages read become double, 80 pages, the pages left become 40, a half.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.2: So no matter how many pages I start reading from, when the pages read double, the pages left are halved.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.3: If you add the pages read and the pages left, it is always 120 pages.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.explain: It is line 3. Lines 1 and 2 match the table and line 4 is also right. But line 3 widened what was right in the one case of going from 40 pages to 80 pages to being right even if the starting page number changes. If you check with other starting page numbers, you can see it is not so.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.prompt: Find cases where Chaea's statement does not hold. Suppose x pages (x is a natural number from 1 to 59) were read at first, and then the pages read became 2x, double. Enter 3 different values of x for which the pages left then are not exactly half of the pages left at first.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.hint.0: Write in a table the pages read at first, the pages left then, and the pages left after reading double.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.hint.1: Compare half of the pages left at first with the pages left after reading double, to see whether they are the same.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 59.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be a natural number from 1 to 59.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.ok.c2: When the pages read are doubled, the pages left are not halved. It is a counterexample.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.fail.c2: When the pages read are doubled, the pages left are exactly halved.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.explain: If x=10, the pages left at first are 110, but after reading 20 pages the pages left are 100 (not 55, which would be half). If x=20, 100 pages become 80, not 50, which would be half. Only 40 pages is the exception, where the pages left 80 become 40.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.prompt: When x=40, Chaea's statement was right. Write how you would fix Chaea's statement, including the relationship that always holds between pages read and pages left.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.hint.0: In the table, write the sum of the pages read and the pages left for each row.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.hint.1: Check once more whether what was right at 40 pages is also right at other page numbers.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with examples (20 pages, 60 pages) that as the pages read increase, the pages left decrease by the same amount, and the sum is constant at 120?
y-m-13-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write separately the case where Chaea's statement was right (40 pages) and the cases where it was not?
y-m-13-12.s.s3.model.0: Even if the pages read double, the pages left are halved only when it is 40 pages. What always holds is that the pages read and the pages left add up to 120.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.model.1: Chaea's statement is right only in the one case of going from 40 pages to 80 pages and is wrong in other cases. You can say that the pages left decrease by as much as the pages read increase, so the sum is always constant at 120 pages.

y-m-13-13.title: How many Go stones are in the 20th level of the triangle?
y-m-13-13.topic: Rules of figure patterns: correspondence where the amount of increase changes
y-m-13-13.goal: In a pattern where the number added changes with each level, find the correspondence between the number of levels and the number of Go stones, apply it to several levels, and compare the method of counting on and the method of finding it with an equation.
y-m-13-13.material: Go stones are stacked in a triangle shape. 1 stone is placed in the top row, 2 in the row below, 3 in the row below that, and so on, so each row down has 1 more stone. The 1-level shape with 1 row has 1 stone in all, the 2-level shape with 2 rows has 3 stones in all, the 3-level shape has 6 stones in all, and the 4-level shape has 10 stones in all. The number of levels is the same as the number of rows.
y-m-13-13.thinking.0: Finding a rule where the amount of increase for each level is not constant
y-m-13-13.thinking.1: Verifying a rule by applying it to several levels
y-m-13-13.thinking.2: Comparing the strengths and weaknesses of two methods
y-m-13-13.prereq.0: Reading a table and explaining how two quantities change together
y-m-13-13.prereq.1: Multiplication and division of natural numbers
y-m-13-13.s.s1.prompt: How many Go stones are needed in all for the 5-level shape?
y-m-13-13.s.s1.hint.0: Write for each level, from level 1 to level 4, the number of stones in the newly placed row.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.hint.1: Find the relationship between the number of stones in the newly placed row and the number of levels, and apply it to level 5.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.o.a: 15 stones: add 5 stones in the bottom row to the 10 stones of level 4.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.r.a: You used the structure that the number of stones in the newly placed row equals the number of levels.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.o.b: 13 stones: assume it increases by 3 for each level and add.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.r.b: Check whether the number added for each level is the same in 1, 3, 6, 10. It went up by 2 from level 1 to level 2; how much did it go up from level 2 to level 3?
y-m-13-13.s.s1.o.c: 20 stones: it is 2 times the 10 of the level 4 shape.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.r.c: The number of levels increased by only one, from 4 to 5. Think about the row added from level 4 to level 5 to see whether the number doubling is right.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.o.d: 16 stones: count by adding 6 to the 10 stones of the level 4 shape.
y-m-13-13.s.s1.r.d: Look at how the number of stones in the newly placed row relates to the number of levels. How many did you add going from level 3 to level 4?
y-m-13-13.s.s1.explain: Each time a new row is placed, the number of stones in that row equals the number of levels. A row of 5 is added to the 10 of the level 4 shape, so the level 5 shape has 15.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.prompt: Say the level n shape needs s Go stones. For levels 5 to 20 (n is a natural number), enter 3 different correct pairs (n, s). You may find them by any method.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.hint.0: Keep adding the number of stones in the newly placed row each level, and find in order the values for levels 5, 6, and 7.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.hint.1: From the values you found, look for whether you can make an equation for the relationship between the number of levels and the number of stones.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.ok.c1: n is a natural number from 5 to 20, and s is a natural number.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 5 to 20.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of stones for that level is right.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.fail.c2: It is different from the number of stones for that level. Calculate again.
y-m-13-13.s.s2.explain: Level 5 is 15, level 6 is 21, level 7 is 28, level 10 is 55, level 20 is 210. It is the sum of all the numbers of stones in the rows from level 1 to level n: 1, 2, 3, …, n. The number of stones at level n can also be found as n×(n+1) divided by 2.
y-m-13-13.s.s3.prompt: There are two friends who want to find the number of Go stones in the level 20 shape. One keeps adding the numbers added at each level starting from level 1, and the other makes an equation from the rule found. Compare the two methods and write what is good about each and what to be careful about.
y-m-13-13.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many times you would have to add if you find level 20 by the method of adding on.
y-m-13-13.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine a scene of checking whether the equation is right using the value of an earlier level (example: level 4).
y-m-13-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both that the method of adding on can be used even if you don't know the rule, and that it is tiring or easy to make mistakes when there are many levels?
y-m-13-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write that the method of finding with an equation is fast, but you need to check whether the equation is right with earlier levels?
y-m-13-13.s.s3.model.0: If you keep adding one at a time, you have to add as many as 20 times, so it takes long and it's easy to make a mistake in the middle. With an equation you can find it at once as 20×21÷2=210, but you have to check first with earlier levels that the equation is right.
y-m-13-13.s.s3.model.1: Adding in order is safe because you can use it even if you don't know the rule, but it is hard when there are many levels. Using an equation is fast, but if you set up the equation wrongly the answer is wrong, so you should test it with the value for level 4 or 5.
